client: I've been really struggling since I started this new marketing job about six weeks ago. The deadlines are relentless, and I constantly feel like I'm the weakest person on the team — everyone else just seems so confident and experienced, and I'm over here barely keeping my head above water. I'm not even sure talking about it is going to change anything, because the pressure is just... real, it's not in my head.
therapist: What you're carrying right now sounds genuinely exhausting — six weeks into a demanding new role, feeling like you're constantly behind while everyone around you seems effortless. I hear both in your words and in the tension in your voice that this isn't just stress you're imagining; the pressure is real, and it makes complete sense that you'd feel stretched thin. What I'd gently offer, though, is that the story you're telling yourself — that you're the *weakest* one there — is worth examining, because being new, feeling uncertain, and struggling to keep up are not the same thing as being inadequate.
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, moderate-paced speech

client: I hear what you're saying, and part of me wants to believe it, but it's hard when I look around and see my colleagues just... handling things that I'm still fumbling through. Like yesterday, my manager asked me a question in a meeting and I completely blanked, and I could see people's faces shift, and that felt like pretty solid evidence that I don't belong there. It's not just a story I'm telling myself — it feels like something I'm living every day.
therapist: The way you're speaking right now — fast, tense, pitched high — tells me this moment from yesterday is still very much alive in your body, not just a memory you're recounting. That blank in the meeting felt humiliating, and I don't want to dismiss that — but I want to gently challenge one piece: you noticed faces *shift*, and your mind immediately wrote the full story that it confirmed you don't belong — is it possible that's one interpretation of an ambiguous moment, rather than hard evidence? Blanking under pressure in week six of a new job is something almost everyone experiences, even the colleagues who look like they're "handling it."
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, very rapid speech

client: I hear what you're saying, and part of me wants to believe that, I really do. But the thing is, it doesn't feel ambiguous to me — it felt very clear in that room, like everyone suddenly saw through me. And even if I'm wrong about what their faces meant, I still blanked, I still couldn't answer a basic question, and that part isn't a story I made up.
therapist: The softness in your voice right now, even as you're holding firm to this, tells me there's something tender underneath this — like you're protecting yourself from getting your hopes up. You're absolutely right that the blank happened — that's real — but I want to separate two things: *blanking on a question* and *not belonging there*, because one is a moment under pressure, and the other is a conclusion about your entire worth on that team. What would you say to a colleague who was six weeks in and froze in a meeting — would that one moment be enough evidence for you to tell them they don't belong?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, soft-spoken, fast speech

client: I'd probably tell that colleague that it happens to everyone, that one moment doesn't define them. But it feels different when it's me — like I hold myself to this completely different standard and I can't figure out how to stop doing that. I know logically what I'd say to someone else, but when I try to apply it to myself it just... doesn't stick, it slides right off.
therapist: The fact that you can see this double standard so clearly — that the compassion you'd freely give a colleague just *slides off* when you turn it toward yourself — is actually a really significant insight, and I can hear in your voice, quick and strained, that even naming it carries some pain. This is one of the most common and most stubborn patterns we work with in CBT: our inner critic holds us to a standard we'd never impose on someone we care about, and it's not a logic problem you can just think your way out of. So rather than trying to force the compassion to "stick," I'm curious — what do you think makes *you* feel like the exception to the grace you so naturally extend to others?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, fast speech

client: I think part of me believes that other people make mistakes because of circumstances, but when I mess up at work it feels like it reveals something fundamentally broken about me. Like my colleague being overwhelmed is understandable, but me being overwhelmed just proves I was never cut out for this in the first place. It's hard to even say that out loud because I know it sounds irrational, but it doesn't feel irrational when I'm in it.
therapist: The way you just said that — fast, high, like the words were almost tumbling out under pressure — tells me how much it costs you to say it out loud, and I want you to know that taking that risk matters. What you've just named has a specific shape in CBT: it's called **personalisation**, this deeply held belief that your struggles reveal a permanent flaw in *you*, while everyone else's struggles are just... weather. That belief isn't irrational — it makes sense given how you've learned to see yourself — but it is a story that was written somewhere along the way, and that means it can be examined and rewritten.
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, very rapid speech

client: I hear what you're saying, and part of me wants to believe that's true, that it's just a story I've been telling myself. But honestly, it doesn't feel like a story, it feels like evidence, like every time I pull away from people or cancel plans because the anxiety gets too loud, I'm just proving the point all over again. How do you rewrite something when it keeps getting confirmed every single day?
therapist: The tension in your voice — fast, high, like you're bracing against something — tells me this question isn't just intellectual for you, it's urgent, almost desperate. But here's what I want to gently name: when anxiety tells you to pull away and cancel plans, and you do, the relief feels like proof you were right to avoid — but what it's actually doing is *protecting the belief* from ever being challenged, which is a cycle CBT calls a **behavioural trap**, not evidence. The story keeps feeling confirmed not because it's true, but because the avoidance never gives reality a chance to write a different ending.
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, fast speech

client: I hear what you're saying, and part of me gets it logically, like I can follow the reasoning. But when I'm actually in that moment, standing in my apartment with my phone in my hand about to text someone to cancel, the relief I feel when I finally do cancel is so overwhelming that it's hard to believe it's just a trap. It feels more like survival than avoidance, you know?
therapist: The way you're speaking — soft, fast, pitched high — even just describing that moment in your apartment carries a kind of quiet anguish, like part of you already knows something important is happening there but it feels too overwhelming to face. And "survival" is exactly the right word for what that relief *feels* like — your nervous system genuinely experiences it as rescue — but what CBT helps us see is that the thing you're being "rescued" from is the anxiety itself, not actual danger, and every time you cancel, your brain learns the threat was real and needs more protecting next time. So the relief isn't lying to you exactly — it's just telling you about the short-term, while quietly making the long-term harder.
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, soft-spoken, fast speech

client: Yeah, I hear what you're saying, and part of me actually gets it logically — like, I can follow the reasoning. But when I'm standing there in my apartment with my hand on the door handle, logic just completely disappears, and all I can feel is this wall of dread that tells me I absolutely cannot walk out that door. It's like knowing the fire alarm is a drill doesn't stop your heart from pounding.
therapist: That image — standing at the door, hand on the handle, the dread just *rising* — and the way you're speaking right now, fast and stretched tight, tells me this isn't abstract for you, this is a moment you've lived recently and your body remembers it. Your fire alarm analogy is actually perfect, and it points to exactly what we'd work on: not making the alarm stop through willpower or logic, but slowly, carefully, teaching your nervous system through *experience* that walking out the door doesn't confirm the danger. That's the work — not thinking your way through the wall, but taking one small step through it while the alarm is ringing, so your brain can collect different evidence than the story it's been building.
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, fast speech

client: Yeah, I hear what you're saying, and part of me gets it logically, but... the idea of just walking through the door while the alarm is going full blast sounds almost cruel to myself, honestly. Like, you're asking me to just stand in the middle of that feeling and not do anything to make it stop, and I don't know if I'm strong enough for that. What if I just freeze completely, or what if it actually makes things worse and I end up more afraid than before?
therapist: The way you're speaking right now — very fast, pitched high, even as the words themselves carry a kind of quiet fear — tells me this question comes from somewhere real and vulnerable, not resistance. And I want to be clear: I'm not asking you to throw yourself into the deep end alone — what CBT actually asks is something much more gradual, like *cracking* the door while the alarm rings, not flinging it open, building tolerance in small steps so your nervous system learns it can survive the feeling. The fear that you'll freeze or come out worse is itself the anxiety talking, trying to protect the wall — but you've already done something hard today, which is sitting with all of this out loud, and that tells me more about your strength than the voice at the door does.
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, very rapid speech

client: I hear what you're saying, and part of me actually wants to believe it — that cracking the door a little is different from being swallowed whole by whatever's on the other side. But I've tried small steps before and somehow they never stay small, like the anxiety just escalates anyway and I end up feeling worse than when I started. So I guess I'm skeptical that my nervous system is actually going to get the memo that it's safe, when it's been screaming the opposite for so long.
therapist: The exhaustion in your voice — fast, high, like you've been holding your breath through this whole conversation — tells me this skepticism isn't stubbornness, it's the scar tissue from having tried and been hurt before, and that deserves real acknowledgment. What you're describing, where small steps seem to escalate anyway, is actually important information — it often means the steps weren't quite structured right, or you were facing them without enough support, not that your nervous system is beyond learning. That's exactly the kind of thing we'd map carefully together, because there's a real difference between exposure that's paced and held, and white-knuckling it alone — and you don't have to figure out which steps to take by yourself.
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, fast speech
